proposals.relationship: Uses Marx’s account of agency under inherited constraints to insist that women helped shape the domestic roles that constrained them.
proposals.evidence_note: In the reprinted1997 retrospective, Cott explicitly applies both halves of Marx’s historical-agency dictum to women. This is her stated interpretive starting point, alongside feminism and other resources. It does not establish sole influence or an independently read Marx original.

proposals.relationship: Adapts Thompson’s distinction between task-oriented work and industrial time discipline to explain the gendering of household labor.
proposals.evidence_note: Cott’s retrospective describes following Thompson’s distinction when studying married women’s continuing household work. Kerber independently identifies E. P. Thompson and the1967 essay in her discussion and note14. Cott’s reproduced name is truncated at a page gap; the specific concept and Kerber’s explicit citation identify E. P., not Dorothy Thompson. Thompson’s original essay remains unread.

proposals.relationship: Credits Scott’s relational account of gender and power in reassessing the study of domesticity.
proposals.evidence_note: Cott’s own1997 note12 singles out Joan W. Scott and the1986 Gender article for elevating relational gender and its relation to power. This is a later assessment, not a claim that the1986 article shaped the1977 book. The page headers jump across the note12 passage in both transcriptions; no exact note-page number is asserted. Scott’s original remains unread.
primary_locators: 1997 note12 in discontinuous segment between displayed xvii and xix

proposals.relationship: Uses Davidoff and Hall’s joint Family Fortunes to connect gender, class formation and the supposed separation of home from public life.
proposals.evidence_note: Cott’s1997 retrospective praises the coauthored1987 study for linking family practices and gender beliefs to middle-class identity and assets, and for challenging the private-home/public-world division. Both authors retain equal credit. The complete supporting paragraph is retained on1997 p.xix; the2020 selection retains note14 at displayed xxvii, without the full corresponding main paragraph. This retrospective use is not a cause of Cott’s1977 book; the original Family Fortunes remains unread.

proposals.relationship: Uses Bederman’s account of discourse to reinterpret domesticity as a contested combination of ideas, practices and power.
proposals.evidence_note: The reprinted1997 retrospective explicitly follows Bederman on discourse exceeding a material-base/ideological-superstructure division and allowing ambiguity and resistance. This is a later conceptual use. The reverse Cott-to-Bederman relationship belongs to Bederman’s dossier and concerns Bederman’s use of earlier Cott books; neither is made the cause of the other’s earlier work.

proposals.relationship: Reframes domesticity retrospectively through a Foucauldian concept of discourse, discussed with Bederman’s mediation.
proposals.evidence_note: Cott expressly states she was not cognizant of this sense of discourse in the early and mid1970s. The1997 retrospective names Foucault and discusses knowledge, power and mutually constitutive practices using Bederman’s exposition. This mediated later reframing is not a claim of direct formative reading or a1977 Foucauldian method. Original Foucault works remain unread.

proposals.relationship: Uses Kerber’s survey to situate later doubts about separate-spheres language in women’s history.
proposals.evidence_note: Cott’s1997 note18 identifies Kerber’s1988 essay as summing up restiveness with separate-spheres rhetoric, within a retrospective reconsideration of categories and gender’s relations to class and race. Nancy Hewitt receives the more direct credit for renovating Cott’s view; that role is not assigned to Kerber. The1997 text is discontinuous, and the precise missing lead-in is not reconstructed.

proposals.relationship: Provides Kerber with an account of domesticity, gendered work and the emergence of feminist consciousness for her history of separate-spheres rhetoric.
proposals.evidence_note: Kerber’s1988 essay devotes a specific discussion to The Bonds of Womanhood, explaining its domesticity/feminism argument and its extension of Thompson’s task/time distinction to married women’s work. This is bounded analytical use rather than blanket endorsement or a formal mentoring claim. The reverse Kerber-to-Cott claim concerns the later1997 retrospective.

proposals.relationship: Recovers Beard’s historical work through a selected edition of her letters, editorial commentary and an introductory assessment.
proposals.evidence_note: Cott’s own1991 preface explains selection, commentary and documentary treatment, including omitted late letters attacking Charles Beard’s critics and the role of the literary heirs. Her introduction treats Mary as a historian in her own right. This is scholarly editorial recovery, not evidence that Mary formally mentored Cott. The full correspondence remains unread.

proposals.relationship: Questions Beard’s treatment of the conflict between domestic responsibilities and women’s opportunities in public life.
proposals.evidence_note: In the selected1991 introduction paragraph beginning She considered, Cott appreciates Beard’s radical challenge to private/public divisions but observes that she looked away from conflicting domestic and public demands. Cott finds her civilizing-power account more comfortable and persuasive for societies with less elaborated public/private divisions. This particular reservation accompanies substantive recovery and praise; it does not reject Beard’s whole work. The source jumps from the displayed48 archive passage to this domesticity paragraph without a connecting page header; its original printed page is uncertain. The next sentence is cut off and supplies no claim.
primary_locators: 1991 introduction, retained paragraph beginning She considered and ending distinctly public or communal; original page uncertain
